purpose: Rituximab-abbs is used to treat certain types of blood cancers, like non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. It is also used for autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis. It helps your body fight the disease by targeting and destroying specific harmful cells.
how_it_works: Your immune system has cells called B-cells, and sometimes these cells can become cancerous or cause your immune system to attack your own body. Rituximab-abbs works like a guided missile — it locks onto a target on the surface of those problem B-cells called CD20. Once attached, it signals your immune system to destroy those harmful cells.
common_side_effects: Infusion reactions (chills, fever, nausea, headache, or low blood pressure during or shortly after the IV drip), fatigue, low blood counts (which can make you more prone to infections or bleeding), nausea, and body aches. Many of these are most common during the first infusion.
warnings: This medication can cause serious infusion reactions, so you will be monitored closely during treatment. It can lower your immune system, making it harder to fight infections — including serious ones like hepatitis B reactivation or a rare but serious brain infection called PML. Tell your doctor right away if you have fever, confusion, or unusual symptoms. Do not use live vaccines while on this medication, and avoid it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an IV infusion (a drip into your vein) at a clinic or hospital — you will not give it to yourself at home. The dose and schedule depend on what condition is being treated. For example, for some cancers it may be given once a week for several weeks, while for rheumatoid arthritis it may be given as two doses about two weeks apart. Your doctor will set the exact schedule for you.
